input.said: What does Seth use the Antikythera mechanism to show?

cases.reply:
He uses it as an early example of computation that isn't digital Turing computation. The article says the earliest computers were analogue devices working in continuous time, not digital Turing machines. The Antikythera mechanism is its first illustration, and the article follows it with cybernetics in the 1950s.

The example sits in the "Other Games In Town" section. That section argues that Turing algorithms are powerful, but many kinds of dynamics and functions go beyond them. The mechanism is a reminder that "computation" has not always meant Turing-style algorithms. This sets up the point that alternative forms of computation are more closely tied to their material basis, and so less substrate-flexible, than standard digital computation. That supports the essay's wider case against computational functionalism, the view that the right computation is enough for consciousness.

The article dates the mechanism to around 2,000 BCE. The article doesn't say so, but my recollection is that it is usually dated to roughly the second century BCE. I haven't verified that, so check it before relying on either date. The date doesn't affect the argument.

input.said: What does Seth say about Chalmers' neural replacement thought experiment?

cases.reply:
Seth thinks the thought experiment fails because its starting premise can't be met. He says it "fails at its first hurdle," since no part of the brain could be swapped for a perfect silicon equivalent [spya-ahtr6e]. In the same passage he describes the experiment as asking us to replace brain parts step by step with silicon parts that work identically. The supposed conclusion is that cognition and consciousness don't depend on what the brain is made of. He also notes that Hinton recently used it to argue conscious AI is already here [spya-ahtr6e].

His reason comes just before. Real brains are tightly integrated across scales, which he calls "generative entrenchment." So you can't assume a single neuron could be replaced by a silicon one while keeping its input-output behavior exactly the same [spya-jnwfxp]. His example is work by Chintaluri and Vogels, who found that some neurons fire spikes apparently to clear metabolic waste. A perfect silicon stand-in would need its own silicon-based metabolism, which he says silicon isn't suited for [spya-un9fjn].

My inference is that he isn't saying the reasoning is invalid. The experiment assumes the replacement preserves function perfectly, and he denies that this can happen. This also ties to his first argument, that brains aren't computers because what they do can't be separated from what they are [spya-zw2m7u].

input.said: What does he say McCulloch and Pitts showed?

cases.reply:
He says McCulloch and Pitts showed in a landmark paper that networks of highly simplified abstract neurons can perform logical operations [spya-va8qxr]. The claim that such networks could in principle run any algorithm comes from later work, by Kleene among others. That work showed the networks were "Turing complete" once given a tape-like memory, as in a Turing machine [spya-va8qxr]. So the "any algorithm" result isn't credited to McCulloch and Pitts themselves. Figure 2's caption shows what their simplified neuron does: it sums weighted inputs and outputs a 1 or a 0 [spya-qknqjx].

Seth uses this to set up his first argument, that brains are not computers. He pairs the result with Turing's work and calls the pair a "mathematical marriage of convenience." You can treat brains as simple networks and ignore their messy biology, and in return you get everything Turing computation offers [spya-v5vz2t]. Today's artificial neural networks are the "children" of that marriage [spya-va72zk].

He then argues the marriage "starts to fall apart" if what brains do can't be separated from what they physically are [spya-p4vmm0]. The McCulloch-Pitts result is therefore the foundation he is arguing against, not a point he disputes.
